red[lane] : -INFINITY; m = warp_max(m); __syncthreads(); for (int j = threadIdx.x; j < ncols; j += 256) s += __expf(xr[j] - m); // pass 2: sum // ... same two-level reduction for s ... for (int j = threadIdx.x; j < ncols; j += 256) yr[j] = __expf(xr[j] - m) * inv; // pass 3 Triton: 9 lines; the whole row is one block of values @triton.jit def softmax(x_ptr, y_ptr, ncols, stride, BLOCK: tl.constexpr): row = tl.program_id(0) # one program per row offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK) mask = offs < ncols x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * stride + offs, mask=mask, other=-float("inf")) x = x - tl.max(x, axis=0) # reduction: compiler's job e = tl.exp(x) tl.store(y_ptr + row * stride + offs, e / tl.sum(e, axis=0), mask=mask) The translations to remember: tl.program_id replaces blockIdx ; tl.arange plus pointer arithmetic plus mask= replace per-thread indexing and bounds checks; tl.load and tl.store move whole blocks (contiguous offsets make them coalesced for free; whether each thread also gets 16-byte vector loads depends on what the compiler can prove: with aligned pointers but a length n that is not a multiple of 16, the same vector add compiles to scalar loads, 16 LDG.E per thread instead of 4 LDG.E.128 compiled here , shown stage by stage in the Compiler stages tab of Triton and Gluon ); tl.max and tl.sum emit the shuffles you wrote by hand; tl.dot is a block matrix multiply that the compiler maps to tensor cores; @triton.autotune searches block sizes, num_warps and num_stages (how many tiles to prefetch) per shape. compiled here : one Triton matmul source compiled without a GPU picks a different tensor-core instruction for each target, HMMA on sm_80 and sm_120, HGMMA (wgmma) on sm_90a and UTCHMMA (tcgen05) on sm_100a; a float32 tl.dot defaults to TF32 tensor cores; a tutorial-style matmul copies tiles with cp.async , not TMA.
